blocks.h2: How a Tankless Water Heater Works
blocks.body: A tankless water heater fires only when you open a hot tap. Water passes through a heat exchanger, gets heated on the spot and goes straight to the fixture. With no stored tank, there's no standby heat loss and no running out. The limit is flow: a unit heats a set number of gallons per minute, so it's sized to how many fixtures you run at once.

blocks.h2: Is Tankless Right for Your Geneva Home?
blocks.intro: A few things decide whether tankless makes sense in your house.

items.body: A wall-mounted unit frees up floor space in a tight older basement.
Tankless units vent through a wall or roof with their own pipe. In older homes with thick masonry walls, we plan the route carefully.
Tankless units need a lot of gas when they fire. We check your line before quoting.
Geneva's water has been softened by reverse osmosis since 2008, which is easier on a heat exchanger. Maintenance still matters.

items.q: Is a tankless heater a good fit for an older home?
items.preview: Often, especially where space is tight.
items.answer: Often. It saves floor space in a tight basement. The main questions are the gas line and the vent path, which we check first.

items.q: Does Geneva's water mean less tankless maintenance?
items.preview: It helps, but it still needs periodic service.
items.answer: Geneva's city water is softened by reverse osmosis to about 5 to 7 grains, which is easier on a heat exchanger than very hard water. Periodic descaling and filter cleaning are still recommended.

items.q: Can one tankless unit run my whole house?
items.answer: Usually. A properly sized unit handles a couple of showers and an appliance at once.

items.q: Will I need a bigger gas line?
items.answer: Sometimes. We check the existing line and include any upgrade in the price.
